summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The protests that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, known as the Monsoon Revolution, mark the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who were previously visible now live in hiding. A Washington Blade assessment of 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, found Bangladesh's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The current national incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022, and the violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is ongoing. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused in the case.

Police extortion is a routine hazard for visibly trans people. After hijra refused to pay extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras in Narayanganj while they collected money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional livelihood. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, which places the country's main transit hub among the documented policing hotspots.

Legal exposure is governed by an ambiguous framework. The Penal Code 1860 criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment; Outright International reports that the provision is rarely enforced as a prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026) states that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within Section 377. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017) reproduces Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for the prosecution of LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013, but that formal recognition has not prevented the rollback of safety in practice since 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The direction of travel since 2022 is upward on every available count: JMBF records 260 violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals in 2025 alone, and characterises the figure as a sharp increase against a trend line that has risen each year since 2022. The 2024 political rupture is the dividing line in the reporting, with Global Press Journal linking the post-revolution gains of hardline conservative Islamist groups to the upending of trans lives.

Formal recognition and lived safety diverge sharply in this jurisdiction. Third-gender identity has been officially recognised since 2013, a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021, and LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held. Against that record, the same sources describe trans people driven into hiding, safe-house locations exposed to mobs, and a community assessed as increasingly vulnerable a year after the change of government.

The evidence base is advocacy and asylum material rather than official statistics. Incident counts come from JMBF, the legal reading comes from Outright International and the UK Home Office, and the account of state-tolerated hostility comes from a UK Upper Tribunal asylum decision drawing on fact-finding missions and IRB Canada material.
localsOnly:
Hijra are legally recognised as a third gender, a status in place since 2014, and gender-marker change is permitted. Recognition is domestic in scope: it governs how residents are documented and recorded inside Bangladesh, and the sources do not describe it as conferring any protection at the border or abroad.

Street-based livelihoods are the point of contact with police for many hijra. Collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates and begging in public both drew arrests in 2024 and 2025, and refusing extortion demands drew a retaliatory attack injuring at least twelve people at Gomdondi Phultala on 10 September 2025. Arrests in Narayanganj on 17 September 2025 followed the same pattern.

Residents who were publicly visible before August 2024 have withdrawn from view. Global Press Journal's featured subject now lives in hiding, and the same reporting describes a safe house for third-gender people whose gate was stormed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Section 377 as applied to lesbianism is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office country policy note records that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision, while ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal and elsewhere described the provision as relevant to all genders. No source in the inventory settles the question.

Whether the murder of Shila on 3 February 2025 was motivated by her trans advocacy is not established in the available material; five unidentified individuals stand accused and the sources do not record a motive or a conviction.

No source in the inventory addresses entry and visa screening of trans visitors, acceptance of passports with altered gender markers at Bangladeshi ports of entry, or access to gender-affirming care while visiting. Those points are not sourced here and should not be read as either permitted or prohibited on the basis of this record.

The 260 incidents and 426 affected individuals for 2025 are JMBF tallies rather than government figures, and no official Bangladeshi crime statistic for anti-trans offences appears in the inventory for comparison.
